title: Finding the nearest car
teaches: Cells and space-filling curves (geohash, quadtrees, S2, H3), a stream of location updates held in memory, and sharding by cell

blocks.text: In 2015 Matt Ranney, then chief systems architect at Uber, gave a talk on how its dispatch system worked. Every driver's phone running the app sent its position to Uber's servers about every four seconds, whether or not the driver had a passenger. A rider opening the app expected to see the nearby cars moving on the map within a second, and a ride request had to find a free car close by and offer it the trip. Both operations required answering one question thousands of times a second: which of the cars moving around this city are near this point right now?

A database answers "find the row with this key" quickly because its index is sorted, and nearness in one dimension matches nearness in the sorted order. A position has two dimensions, latitude and longitude, and no single sort order keeps every pair of nearby points together. In this lesson, we will examine techniques that approximate a two-dimensional sort by cutting the map into cells and numbering them so that nearby cells usually receive nearby numbers. This numbering turns a spatial query into a few lookups in an ordinary sorted or hashed store. In lesson M1, we cut the map into tiles named by zoom, column and row, but those tiles lacked a single number in which nearby tiles received nearby values.

We can start by calculating the load. Suppose one million drivers are online during the busiest hour, and each sends a position every four seconds, generating 250,000 updates a second. An update consists of a driver's ID, a latitude, a longitude, a timestamp and a state (free, offered a trip, or carrying a passenger). At about 50 bytes per update, 12.5 MB a second of data arrives. Each update replaces the previous one from the same driver, and a position is stale after 30 seconds. The entire live dataset is one million records of 50 bytes, or 50 MB, which fits easily in the memory of a single ordinary server. Read requests are less frequent, but each one is a spatial search, peaking at around 100,000 searches a second.

The first design you might consider is a table of drivers in a relational database, with one index on latitude and another on longitude, queried for rows whose latitude and longitude both fall within a small bounding box around the rider. This approach fails for two reasons. First, an index on latitude narrows the search only to a band around the entire planet. The latitudes of Manhattan run through Spain, Italy, Turkey and northern China, and every driver along that band remains a candidate until the longitude check filters them out. Second, each of the 250,000 updates a second rewrites two index entries on disk and in a write-ahead log for data that will be overwritten four seconds later. You should keep live positions in memory, and append a copy to an append-only log such as Kafka (lesson 16) for systems that need the historical trace.

In 2008 Gustavo Niemeyer published **geohash**, which encodes a geographic position into a short string.[^geohash] The algorithm halves the longitude range and writes a 1 if the point falls in the eastern half or a 0 if it falls in the western half. It then halves the latitude range in the same way, alternating between longitude and latitude so that each bit halves the cell's area. The bits are encoded five at a time as characters from a 32-character alphabet. Each additional character divides the cell's area by 32. At the equator, five characters name a cell about 4.9 km on a side, six characters name a cell of about 1.2 km by 0.6 km, and seven characters name a cell of about 150 m on a side. Points in the same cell share a prefix, so a key-value store sorted by geohash keeps each cell's drivers contiguous, and reading a cell's drivers requires a single range scan.

Two problems follow from this grid. The first is boundary effects. Two cars 1 m apart on opposite sides of a cell boundary sit in different cells, and at the largest boundaries, the equator or the prime meridian, their geohashes do not even share a first character. Because of this, a search cannot scan only the rider's cell. It must scan every cell that the search circle intersects, which for a circle smaller than a cell means scanning the rider's cell and up to eight surrounding cells. The second problem is that a single cell size does not suit an entire country. A cell size that holds three drivers in Montana will hold three hundred drivers in Manhattan at 18:00.

A **quadtree** (Raphael Finkel and Jon Bentley, 1974) adapts to varying density. You start with one square, and whenever a square holds more than a set maximum number of points, you split it into four smaller squares. Cities are subdivided into fine cells and rural areas remain coarse, so every leaf cell holds roughly the same number of drivers. **Hexagons** solve a different problem: the centres of a square's four edge neighbours are 1 cell width from its own centre, while the centres of its four corner neighbours are about 1.41 cell widths away. All six of a hexagon's neighbours have centres at the exact same distance, which makes hexagonal grids better for smoothing rider or driver counts over an area.

blocks.caption: 400 drivers on a 20 km square, most of them in a city centre, and a search for those within 1.5 km of the blue point. Shaded cells are the ones the search must scan. Tap the map to move the search.
blocks.task: Try each way of cutting the map

blocks.text: In the city centre, a fixed grid of 2.5 km squares forces a search to scan a few hundred drivers to find the few dozen within 1.5 km, whereas the quadtree's smaller city cells require scanning far fewer drivers. If you move the search into the countryside, both the fixed grid and the quadtree scan nearly empty cells. The drawback of a dynamic quadtree is that its cell boundaries shift as drivers move, so the system must continuously update or rebuild the tree every few seconds.

Geohash numbers its cells along a **Z-order curve**: interleaving the longitude and latitude bits visits the four quadrants of a square in the shape of the letter Z, and recursively visits each quadrant's sub-quadrants in the same order. Cells that are adjacent in the numbering are usually adjacent on the map, but the curve makes long diagonal jumps from the end of one Z to the start of the next, giving some adjacent cells on the map numbers that are far apart.

Google's **S2** library, written by Eric Veach, numbers cells along a **Hilbert curve** instead. This space-filling curve visits every cell of a grid while only ever stepping to an immediate edge neighbour, ensuring that consecutive numbers always correspond to adjacent cells.[^hilbert] S2 encloses the Earth in a cube, projects each of the cube's six faces onto the sphere, and subdivides each face as a quadtree up to 30 levels deep, where a leaf cell is about 1 cm across. A cell's 64-bit ID encodes its cube face and its path down the tree in Hilbert order. The library approximates any query region, such as a circle around a rider or the boundary of a city, with a **covering** consisting of a small set of cells of mixed sizes, which translates into a small number of ID ranges.

blocks.caption: An 8 by 8 grid numbered along a Z-order curve and along a Hilbert curve, and a search over 9 cells. Each run of consecutive numbers is one range scan in a store sorted by cell number.
blocks.task: Switch to the Hilbert curve and move the search about

blocks.text: This numbering allows us to store spatial data in the databases from earlier lessons. Bigtable (lesson 10) keeps rows sorted by key, so a table keyed by the S2 cell ID concatenated with the item's ID can return everything in a region using a few range scans. A hash-partitioned store such as Dynamo (lesson 12) cannot perform range scans, but it can store one record per cell containing the list of drivers inside it, allowing a search to fetch the cells of its covering by their exact keys.

Uber open-sourced its own spatial index, **H3**, in 2018. H3 covers the Earth with hexagons at 16 resolutions, ranging from cells with edges about 1,100 km long down to cells with edges under 1 m, with each cell containing roughly seven child cells at the next resolution down.[^pentagons] Uber uses H3 to aggregate supply and demand across a city, to calculate surge pricing by area and to forecast load, which are tasks where uniform distance to every neighbour prevents distortion. For finding the nearest car, square cells in a sorted store are simpler to query; for aggregating metrics across a city, hexagons avoid directional bias.

The live index is two maps in memory. One maps each driver's ID to its latest record: cell, position, time and state. The other maps each cell to the set of drivers in it. An update looks up the driver; if the cell has changed, it moves the driver from one set to the other; then it overwrites the record. A driver not heard from for thirty seconds is dropped. A search computes the cells its circle touches, reads their sets, checks each driver's true distance and state, and ranks the free ones by estimated time to reach the rider, which lesson M3 shows how to compute. The cell size is chosen per search: S2 picks the level whose cells are about the size of the circle, so a covering is at most eight or so cells. A search for the k nearest free cars has no radius to start with. It reads the rider's cells; if it finds fewer than k, or the k-th is farther away than the edge of the area read, a nearer car could lie just outside, so it widens the ring of cells and reads again.

A single server has enough memory to hold the entire index, but it cannot process 250,000 updates and 100,000 searches a second with safe headroom, nor can it survive a hardware failure on its own. Instead, we shard the index by cell across many servers, assigning each server a subset of cells using consistent hashing (lessons 5 and 12). Uber built the Ringpop library to manage this sharding: servers discover each other and track cluster membership via a gossip protocol, place themselves on a hash ring, and forward any incoming request to the server that owns the target cell.[^swim] A search whose query circle overlaps cells on two or three servers queries each of them in parallel, requiring a small fan-out. As we saw in lesson 9, a fanned-out request must wait for the slowest responding server, which adds minimal tail latency when fanning out to only two or three nodes.

Sharding by cell suffers from the same hotspot problem as the timestamp-prefixed row keys in lesson 10. Request load follows the cells, and the cells do not receive equal traffic. During rush hour, a city centre directs a large fraction of the updates to the few servers that own its cells.

blocks.caption: Position updates hashed by cell to four shards, in slow motion. With one cell size, the city centre is a few busy cells; with cells cut smaller where drivers are dense, its load spreads over many.
blocks.task: Raise the updates to 400 a second or more, then cut busy cells smaller

blocks.text: Suppose we scale the system tenfold to handle 2.5 million updates a second. If one in-memory server handles 100,000 updates a second, we need 25 shards, and a spatial search still queries only the two or three servers that own the relevant cells. Scaling a hundredfold to 25 million updates a second requires 250 shards, while a search still touches only two or three servers. The bottleneck is a dense city, and we can fix it by applying the quadtree concept to our sharding scheme: we subdivide high-traffic cells into smaller cells at a deeper S2 level so that a busy city centre hashes across many servers, while leaving rural areas in large cells.

Dispatching the nearest free car to each rider in order of request is not always optimal. Suppose rider A requests a ride first, when driver X is 2 minutes away from A and driver Y is 3 minutes away. A moment later rider B requests a ride, and B is 2 minutes from X but 10 minutes from Y. Assigning each rider the nearest free car as the requests arrive gives car X to rider A and leaves car Y for rider B, requiring 2 + 10 = 12 minutes of driving to pick up both riders. If the system instead waits 2 seconds, collects both requests, and matches them together, it assigns car Y to rider A and car X to rider B, requiring 3 + 2 = 5 minutes of driving. Batching trades a few seconds of waiting latency for a large reduction in total driving time across the city, turning dispatch into a bipartite matching problem solved over each batch.

Once the system selects a match, it sends an offer to the chosen driver, who has a few seconds to accept before the system moves on to the next candidate. The dispatch system must never offer the same driver two trips at the same time. We can prevent double-booking using the atomic operations from lesson 11: the server owning the driver's record updates the driver's state from free to offered using a compare-and-swap operation, ensuring that if two concurrent searches select the same free driver, only one succeeds.

blocks.title: The shape of the design
points: Positions are overwritten every few seconds: keep them in memory, and log a copy.
Cells turn two dimensions into keys; search every cell the circle touches, not just one.
A Hilbert-ordered cell ID makes a region a few range scans in a sorted store.
Shard by cell, and cut cells finer where drivers are dense.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on finding what is nearby
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Two cars are 1 m apart, but their geohashes share no prefix at all. What explains this?
choices: Geohash rounds positions to the nearest kilometre, so close points can land anywhere
One of the cars sent its position in degrees and the other in radians
They sit on opposite sides of a major cell boundary, such as the equator
items.why: Points in the same cell share a prefix, but nearby points across a boundary can fall into cells whose names differ starting from the very first character. Because of this, a search must scan every cell that its query circle touches.

items.ask: One million drivers each send a position every 4 seconds. How many updates a second must the system handle, and where should it store the latest positions?
choices: 250,000 updates a second, in memory, with a copy appended to a log
4 million updates a second, on disk in an indexed table
25,000 updates a second, in a relational table with indexes on latitude and longitude
items.why: 1,000,000 ÷ 4 s = 250,000 updates a second. Each update overwrites the previous position and becomes stale within seconds, so in-memory storage suits the live workload while an append-only log preserves the history.

items.ask: Why does a database table indexed on latitude perform poorly when answering "find drivers within 2 km of this point"?
choices: Latitude cannot be stored in an index, because it is a floating-point number
The latitude index narrows the search only to a band around the entire planet
An index on latitude sorts drivers by distance from the equator, not from the rider
items.why: A 4 km band of latitudes circles the globe across every longitude, so the query must scan every driver in every city along that band before filtering them by longitude.

items.ask: Why is a quadtree a better fit than a fixed grid for indexing drivers spread across a country?
choices: It needs no updating as drivers move, because its cells never change
It gives every cell six neighbours at equal distances, which a grid cannot
It splits cells where drivers are dense, so each cell holds roughly the same number of drivers
items.why: In a fixed grid, city cells hold hundreds of drivers while rural cells sit empty. A quadtree adapts its cell size to the local density, at the cost of updating the tree as drivers move.

items.ask: What advantage does numbering cells along a Hilbert curve provide to a database sorted by cell ID?
choices: Every cell's ID is shorter, so the store holds more cells in the same memory and scans faster
Consecutive IDs always represent neighbouring cells, so a two-dimensional region maps to a few range scans
Each cell's four neighbours have IDs one apart, so any circular search is a single range scan
items.why: The Hilbert curve never jumps across the map, so nearby cells group into a small number of contiguous ID runs. Because no one-dimensional curve can make all four neighbours consecutive in two dimensions, a search still requires several range scans.

items.ask: Driver positions are sharded by cell. At rush hour, the single server that owns the city centre's few cells is overloaded while the other servers sit idle. What is the best fix?
choices: Subdivide the busy cells into smaller cells, so the city centre's load spreads across more servers
Add more servers to the ring, keeping every cell at the size it is now
Send each update to every server, so any of them can answer any search
items.why: A single hot cell maps to one server regardless of how many servers are on the hash ring, so adding servers does not split a hot cell's load. Subdividing dense areas into finer cells turns a few hot keys into many keys, which consistent hashing distributes across the cluster.

items.ask: With two riders and two drivers, rider A is 2 minutes from driver X and 3 minutes from driver Y, while rider B is 2 minutes from driver X and 10 minutes from driver Y. Rider A requests a ride first. Which assignment is better, and how does the system find it?
choices: A gets X and B gets Y, 12 minutes in all, found by giving each rider the nearest free car
A gets X and B waits for X to finish, found by queueing riders for the nearest car
A gets Y and B gets X, 5 minutes in all, found by matching a short batch of requests together
items.why: Greedy matching assigns the nearest car to A and leaves B with a car 10 minutes away. Batching requests over a couple of seconds and solving the assignment problem across the batch reduces the total pickup time from 12 minutes to 5 minutes.

summary: **Calculate the load before choosing a database.** One million drivers sending updates every 4 seconds generates 250,000 updates a second of data that expires within seconds, so you should hold the current state in memory and append a copy to a log.
**Separate indexes on latitude and longitude perform poorly.** A latitude range selects a band around the entire planet, and high-frequency updates constantly rewrite the on-disk indexes.
**Spatial cells convert a two-dimensional coordinate into a one-dimensional key.** Geohash interleaves the bits of longitude and latitude so that points within the same cell share a string prefix.
**Query every cell that intersects the search radius.** Nearby points on opposite sides of a cell boundary can have completely different cell prefixes.

**A quadtree adapts cell size to point density, while hexagons provide equidistant neighbours.** Subdivide cells finely in cities and coarsely in rural areas, and use hexagonal grids when smoothing demand counts across a map.
**S2 numbers cells along a Hilbert curve.** Any geographic region maps to a covering of a few cells, which translates into a few range scans in a sorted key-value store.
**Shard by cell and subdivide hot cells.** Because update traffic follows driver density, split busy city cells at a finer resolution to spread their load across more servers.
**Batch matching outperforms greedy nearest-neighbour dispatch.** Collecting requests for a couple of seconds and solving the assignment problem across the batch reduces total driving time.

geohash.title: A short link for a place
geohash.text: Niemeyer launched geohash as a public web service at geohash.org to provide short URLs for geographic coordinates, much as TinyURL (lesson 3) provided short links for web pages. Encoding a coordinate as a short alphanumeric string that could be pasted into a URL came first; using those strings as database keys came later.

hilbert.title: Hilbert's curve
hilbert.text: David Hilbert described his space-filling curve in 1891 as a mathematical curiosity: if you repeat its recursive construction infinitely, the one-dimensional line passes through every point in a two-dimensional square. Spatial indexes stop after a fixed number of subdivisions, producing a path that visits every cell of a grid without ever jumping to a non-adjacent cell.

pentagons.title: Twelve pentagons
pentagons.text: A sphere cannot be tiled using hexagons alone. H3 starts with a regular icosahedron (a polyhedron with 20 triangular faces) and places a pentagon at each of its 12 vertices, orienting the icosahedron so that all 12 pentagons fall in the oceans. These 12 pentagons remain at every resolution. Because a hexagon's seven child cells do not perfectly tile its boundary, a parent cell's area is only approximately equal to the sum of its seven children's areas.

swim.title: Gossip
swim.text: Ringpop's membership protocol was based on SWIM (Abhinandan Das, Indranil Gupta and Ashish Motivala, 2002). Each server periodically pings a randomly chosen peer, asks a few other peers to probe the target if the ping times out, and piggybacks cluster membership changes onto its ping messages. News of a server joining or failing reaches the entire cluster in a few rounds without requiring a central coordinator.
